utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, may we have the appearances please. For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President. Kenneth Scott --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. Full Prosecution team, who I think you're familiar with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mladen Naletilic, we are in the same composition. I think you all know us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the record, let me say I'm lawyer Branko Seric and my co-counsel is my colleague, Mr. Zelimir Par. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Martinovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED MARTINOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I won't ask you the same question every morning. If you have any problems in the future, just let us know. You may sit down, please. Mr. Naletilic, can you hear the proceedings in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We won't ask you the same question in the future. If you have any problems, please let us know. THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we are very sorry for the delay. I guess it happens every time on the first day. Before we start the Defence case, are there any procedural issues that both parties would like to bring to the attention of the Chamber? Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not for the Prosecution, Your Honour, other than various outstanding matters which the Chamber is already aware of. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Except the ongoing motions, we have no other procedural matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand that you filed a motion asking for the closed session for your first witness. We would like to hear the response from the Prosecution on this motion for the closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, as we announced last week in the Status Conference, we expect to respond generally quite liberally, if I can use that term, to the Defence request for protective measures for their witnesses to the extent that they are roughly commensurate with the protective measures that were granted to the Prosecution witnesses. I think it's fair to say that in most instances, if it was a matter of pseudonym and facial distortion, those have been granted rather -- I wouldn't want to say freely, but often, and we do not expect to have objections to that. However, as the Chamber knows, closed session raises additional issues, and I think the record will reflect - and I didn't make a count - but I think the record will reflect that very, very few Prosecution witnesses actually testified in closed session, in contrast to other protective measures. As to this witness, the first witness, Your Honours, we do not see any adequate justification for closed session for this witness. There is nothing that indicates that there is any sort of imminent risk or danger to him, and of course I won't say anything more about -- to identify the person. This is a person who has taken - again, I'll be very careful what I say - but public positions in the past, and to that extent, should not be bashful about taking public positions here in this Court. So our position is, Your Honour, we would not be opposed to a pseudonym, if that might be helpful, but we think closed session is not appropriate for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik, if you need private session, we will just simply go into private session for this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, not for the moment. All I want, as I say, is that we wrote a supplement to the motion for closed session so I don't know whether the Prosecution has received a copy. We did write the supplement, I believe on Friday, as we learnt of new facts -- we learnt some new facts that day which indicate the jeopardy, not of the individual themselves. May we go into private session for a moment for me to explain? Because I have to try and explain what I mean, what it's all about. If we might go into private session for a moment, if you have not received the supplement to our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session. Mr. Krsnik, are you ready for your opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please tell us how long it will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would gladly tell you, but in preparing for this opening statement, I and my team tried to calculate how long it would take, because we did have a dress rehearsal, but I'm afraid we weren't able to calculate how long it would take. I have some videotapes, I have some maps to show, and all the other material, and although it is brief, it is nonetheless an opening statement. But I think that it will take between two and three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but may I just say that the videotapes and all the other documents or books that I will be referring to briefly and showing briefly, they only serve to give a general picture. I'm not going to tender them into evidence at all today. What I shall be tendering into evidence, I will do with the help of each witness, and the numbers that the documents have been assigned. I'll do that in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you this question just because to properly arrange the time at our disposal. We have to finish by 1.45 today. And the -- since we had a very late start, so maybe we'll have a break every hour, every 60 minutes. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gave great thought as to how to begin my opening statement. This is the first time in my career that that has happened, and in this way and for this trial. Let me say at the outset, in advance, that I'm going to present evidence and call witnesses. We will put them forth and bring them forth before this Honourable Tribunal. Never before in my experience and practice as a lawyer did I have this opportunity, so I prepared at length precisely for that reason and precisely because everything I'm going to say today, here and now, will be presented before this Tribunal, both viva voce, through the witnesses themselves, and by providing material evidence: documents, geographical maps, or videotapes. And this evidence had to be selected. We selected witnesses who have direct knowledge, and we will not bring forward a single witness who will testify at secondhand or with hearsay. Conscious of what I have stated, and if I do not act as I have said I would, then this opening statement of mine would remain hanging in the air, if I can put it that way, or it will be a mere attempt to impress someone, to impress someone with something that later on I will not be able to prove or to demonstrate or to call in evidence. I'm not going to hurl and bandy lofty conclusions, high-sounding, highfalutin, nor will I engage in political debate. The Defence has truly collected and amassed, through great effort, more than sufficient number of evidence and proof; however, it is confronted with an enormous task. There is the three of us, only the three of us, and it is the three of us that will stand up to the enormous apparatus and power and potential, that is not controlled through any means, that stands across the well from us on the opposite side. As the indictment represents, unfortunately, only one untested angle of vision, relying on only one side, looking at it from one aspect, the Bosniaks, I wish to clarify some terminology first in this regard. The Defence -- up until the Washington Agreement itself, at the beginning of 1994, the constitutional legal term was "Muslims," and I'm going to refer to these people as Muslims. After the Washington Agreement, when all legal acts were recognised and defacto international recognition was given, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna incorporated the Bosniaks as a nation, or Bosniakhood, and the Bosniak language along with it. So that is what I wanted to clarify at the very outset, the terminology that I am going to use, as a man of the law and a lawyer, and in keeping with positive legal rules and regulations and laws. Therefore, the Prosecution, viewing the whole case in a subjective manner and providing evidence accordingly, has done what it has done. The Defence is going to try and call into question this angle and will show, through witnesses, that the events that took place were viewed from a very subjective angle of vision, but also that it was controlled from a highly interested circle, to whom it is of no little importance whether they will be shown to be and demonstrated to be the sole victim, as the sole victims in the events that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina and, at the same time, with close cooperation with the Prosecution, which goes along the route of AID, to cover up its criminal behaviour with the formula of what the ordinary people would refer to as "Catch the thief," "Let's catch the thief." So because of what I have said thus far, I wish to stress that it is my privilege to be the Defence counsel of Mladen Naletilic before this Tribunal, especially as the system, the vast system, enormous system, turns against an individual and comes at the individual with all its power and might. It is an unjust balance of forces. And that is why it is my pleasure and privilege, together with my client, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, to challenge the allegations and indictment and accusations of the system, which before this Tribunal, is being presented by the Prosecution. This is the first trial, the first case, in which we are discussing the conflict between the HVO and the BiH army in the area of Herzegovina, on the territory of Herzegovina, and the Defence, by presenting its evidence, will present the events from 1990 onwards, that is to say from the first multi-party elections that took place up until February, 1994. The Defence of Mladen Naletilic is duty-bound but also has the right to present its evidence and in doing so to challenge the counts and accusations in the indictment, the annex of the indictment and the introductory statement made by the Prosecution, the opening statement. Similarly, it will challenge the evidence put forward by the Prosecution in its case, in the Prosecution case, against the accused and refers directly to Mladen Naletilic. At the very beginning, I wish to emphasise the following. It is my profound conviction that this Honourable Trial Chamber, despite the already-passed judgements but that are not in power yet, will not be closed to arguments and proof and evidence which the Defence will put forward with respect to the existence of an international armed conflict and persecution. The Defence feels it incumbent upon itself to present evidence which will throw light on the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina immediately after the multi-party elections were held and to show the formation and development of the political parties, their programmes and aims, as well as the development of the relationships between all three ethnic groups in the BiH. That is to say, the causes of the conflict, and the results of that conflict. Your Honours, unless we set out in this direction - and we are only talking about a ten year period of history - we cannot understand the cause-and-effect relationship, and even less, being so far away from the events, because they occurred a long way off, we cannot learn of them in a mere four-hour testimony by an expert witness, for example, or understand what happened or be able to understand what happened just ten years ago, let alone 100 years ago or 500 years back in the past. The Defence will, of course, only be speaking about 1990 and onwards, just ten years previously, and will be presenting evidence in that respect, and being guided by many of the wisdoms that we have heard here, the advice I have been given as to how I should proceed in my work, and the guidelines. Bearing all that in mind, I shall endeavour to do my job. Let me refer to our very honourable and distinguished President of the Trial Chamber, and let me say that Rome was not built in seven days, as he pointed out, and therefore, guided by that, and all Your Honours' other guidelines and instructions, we shall attempt in the briefest possible way, but by presenting forceful arguments and evidence, we shall try to challenge the indictment and the accusations and counts that were made about events that took place ten years ago. The Defence is also duty-bound to challenge Mladen Naletilic's acts, especially crimes against humanity, the counts against him, persecutions under Article 5 of the Statute, and the distinguished Prosecution claims that all the acts were committed at the time when, on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there existed partial occupation by Croatia and that there existed an international armed conflict. And let's take things in order, first things first. First and foremost, the Defence will try and clarify, by presenting evidence, the role of AID in this trial and in these proceedings, but not only in them, because it is indisputable, and has been established as being so, and that is the reason why the Defence will present evidence in that direction, and according to the statements of the investigator himself, the OTP investigator, and according to their own recognition here in the courtroom, that the closest cooperation on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, generally -- was generally with the AID. These were the closest ties they had. Therefore, we have to answer the question, and we shall do so, what is AID? Who is AID? The Defence will move to show that the AID is a political, exclusively Muslim, secret police, which they created and incorporated into the system of the SDA party. Its real name is the Agency for Research and Documentation -- Investigation and Documentation. And so with this almost-euphemistic term, it seems to say that it is dealing with the investigation of war crimes and similar matters, thereby masking its true activities or making them appear lesser or masking the truth of its actions, especially during the times of war, but also after the war came to an end, right until the present day. It deals with intelligence work, in fact, special warfare, planting disinformation and everything else, and all the other things that every intelligence service and secret service throughout the world does, which is their job, in fact. Of course, this Tribunal is in the focus of its attentions, and we could see this, Your Honours, from what has been presented so far. The witnesses that were called here, I can't give you a percentage, but we'll agree that at least 70 per cent of the witnesses and their first encounters and first statements were to that agency. Its activities were, of course, in the interests of only one peoples, that is to say, the Bosniak peoples, against the others, with the aim of creating, painting a picture - and that is part of special warfare too, which I enumerated a moment ago - that the HZ and HB, the HR HB, and the HVO, were illegal occupying forces and that the Republic of Croatia had the intentions, clearly defined intentions, in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In preparing the witnesses for this trial, by suggesting to them that they should paint a picture of the type I have described through their testimony, because it is a false picture which covers the true aims of the SDA party, and those aims were to put into effect the Islamic declaration premises, and I'll be speaking at length about that a little later on. It was incorporated -- the Islamic declaration was incorporated into the SDA party programme and platform, preparations for the creation of an Islamic state, and in my opening statement I will be speaking extensively about that too, and the Islamisation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by showing it to be no more, no less, but a government, a government, if you will, force, and the HVO is being presented as a non-government force. The President of the SDA, that gentleman, and the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, they are showing as being the legally elected president, if you will, up until the first free elections after the Dayton Peace Agreement, consciously masking the fact that he had to leave the position of President of the Presidency, he had to step down from that position in December 1992 because at that time, according to the constitution that was in force, his second mandate had expired as President of the Presidency and he was no longer able to perform that function. However, this is something that he did not do. He manipulated in the Presidency, he was manipulative, and he manipulated for a further five years. He replaced and elected members of the Presidency in accordance with his own desires, but he selected exclusively those who would listen to him. However, as far as the constitution is concerned and the legality of the matter, this has nothing to do - and this is something that the Defence will show - only those who have no idea about this can believe that this is a constitutional, legal matter, only those who have nothing -- who are not aware of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And they didn't try to find out, and they never asked anyone else to clarify this to them, although they could have done so and they still can do so, in order to ensure that the historical truth, which can't be falsified by any judgement, should not be concealed and should be discovered in time. In such a case, we wouldn't lose so much time in this Tribunal in an attempt to prove something that is a well-known fact, and it is a well-known fact that the HVO was an absolutely legal military organisation of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a well-known fact, and I will use documents to show this to you today, here in the Trial Chamber, and I will use witnesses in the following days to prove this. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina is being presented here as if it were the government, perhaps, of some European country, or perhaps of the United States of America, as if it functioned in such a way at the time of war. The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina ceased to exist when a state of war was declared in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because in accordance with the constitution which was in force, a War Presidency is established in which the following members -- Please, could you show this on the ELMO. As you can see on these screens, the legally elected members, they're elected by majority. The only legal, legally elected presidency, elected in elections in 1990 and which is composed of seven members and due to the number of votes that they obtained, two presidents, two representatives, are elected from each constituent people, because here, before this respected Tribunal, at times we were surprised by having to say and produce evidence that there were three peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this presidency was thus elected and there were two Croats, two Serbs, two Bosniaks and one person who was a member of the Yugoslavs, or that is to say of "others," that is to say ethnic minorities. So if we go -- take this in order, for the Bosniaks, there is Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. Fikret Abdic, who received the largest number of votes at the elections, but through the manipulation of the SDA party, he did not become the President. And in 1990, there were indications, and Alija Izetbegovic was constantly hypocritical, was two-faced. The representatives of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Professor Nikola Koljevic, Professor Biljana Plavsic. From the Croatian people, a representative of the Croatian people, the journalist, a sports journalist, and president of the Table-Tennis Association of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Stjepan Kljuic, who later was also a president of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Here we have Franjo Boras. And after this first manipulation, there was a second one. Fikret Abdic, although he received the largest number of votes, did not become the President, and as a representative of the Yugoslavs - and this included people who did not declare themselves to be Serbs or Croats or Muslims, but they simply felt themselves to be Yugoslavs because they came from mixed marriages or they had personal convictions of their own, or from ethnic minorities, let's say the Czechs, the Slovaks, the Bulgarians, the Jews. No, the SDA party, by manipulating - because at the time they would call themselves Yugoslavs - Mr. Ejub Ganic, although he was a Muslim and a member of the SDA party, and these people, this people, already had two representatives in the presidency, nevertheless he was elected, and in subsequent events, he played a very important role. He was an intimate associate of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and he very rapidly became, not even one year later - and this is something that we will clarify - when Alija Izetbegovic was returning from Lisbon and was briefly arrested by the Yugoslav People's Army, instead of replacing him and transferring duties to the next person who should be the President in -- because of the majority of votes obtained, such as was the case with Fikret Abdic, no, he selected Mr. Ganic and authorised him to replace him while he was under arrest, and in this manner he made it clear, because he was a president of all the three peoples, the first among equals in the presidency, and he had no other authorities other than being the first among equals. He took over the power and gave it to Ejub Ganic, and it was clearly made known to Bosnia and Herzegovina what direction this was leading in. And it was no later than the end of 1991. At the time, many called this a coup d'etat. I will now briefly turn to all the manipulations and all the unconstitutional, illegitimate acts of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic in this War Presidency, and we shall clearly show all of this in this Tribunal. But I forgot to say, the government ceased to exist. I'm sorry I went off on a tangent because of this photograph. So into this War Presidency, in accordance with their positions, the following entered, the President of the government, it was -- it was, I think, the Croat Mr. Jure Pelivan, because there was a constitutional principle according to which rotation was carried out, so a representative of each people would be enabled to have a mandate which could be extended for one year at the most, it could be the president of the presidency, of the government, of the Assembly. The President of the Assembly entered this in accordance with his position, and the commander of the Territorial Defence. Your Honour, when I was thinking about how to present this opening statement, I knew that the most difficult thing would be to make it interesting and not to tire you, but when I start thinking about all the subjects that I should neglect, I realised that it would be necessary to explain what the Territorial Defence is because I'm sure you don't know this and you don't know how it was formed and what its function was in the SFRY. And this term was used and manipulated and a lot of false words were said about it. But it had a very clear, legally prescribed role. For all the citizens in the then Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, its role was very clear, and its task was very clear and well defined. According to the conception of a general defensive war, which dates back to the Russian -- to the Georgian war and to the partisan war, at the time of the late Marshal Tito, on this basis the Territorial Defence organisation was established, and this means that all the employees of a factory or of a company would buy weapons with their own funds, and they would keep these weapons either in the companies. And people who had done their military service, in the event of war, had the duty naturally to serve and to be mobilised by the Territorial Defence, their weapons were kept in the depots of the Yugoslav People's Army. Thus each republic, which was pretending to have a certain state-forming characteristics in the then Yugoslavia, each republic had its commander of the Territorial Defence and usually they were retired generals of the Yugoslav People's Army, and they thus represented the armed forces of a certain republic. Naturally, you can come to the logical conclusion, what was the first thing that the JNA did? The weapons of the Territorial Defence that it had in its barracks, of course it kept them but it gathered all the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. arms, all the weapons, that were outside of the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army, in preparations for aggression against the Republic of Croatia - you will now see I'll be using different terms - and for the conquering of territory, for the seizure of territory, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this is how the civil war started, and I will elaborate on this in my statement. There was a civil war for territory. In the first phase, the Muslims and Croats were defending territory together. They were defending it from Serbian aggression. And subsequently, they were unfortunately attacked by the BH Army, which nowhere from 1992, and right up until 1995, when they fought again with the HVO, they didn't liberate a single square metre in the direction towards the Serbs. But they fought against those who were weaker and carried out aggression under the control of -- against territory under the control of the HVO, and in order to obtain - and you will see how absurd this is - the best possible initial position, in order to obtain a head start, and this was done under the auspices of the international community. So the commander of the TO entered the Territorial Defence, and Alija Izetbegovic naturally did not like this. He entered this -- he obtained this position by virtue of his office. He temporarily replaced him. Sorry, I can't remember the name right now, but a Bosniak came and he became the commander of the Territorial Defence. As soon as he had been replaced, he also brought in Mr. Sefer Halilovic, and this had nothing to do with the constitutional regulations and legal regulations. He was a citizen of another republic at that time, of another state at that time. He was listed as a citizen of the Republic of Serbia at that time. You'll see why I emphasise this, because I'm going to draw a parallel with Croatia too later on. Naturally, he represented the interests of those who at the beginning agreed with Alija Izetbegovic, but it's necessary to speak the truth and say that he was opposed to the Islamisation which was becoming increasingly noticeable as time passed. He came into conflict with Alija Izetbegovic as the supreme commander of the army. He resisted such Islamisation, and for this reason, he was replaced. Rasim Delic became the head of the army. He only had one commander, and he said that only Alija Izetbegovic could give him orders and no one else. The fate of Mr. Sefer Halilovic was tragic after that. There was an attempt at an assassination. A rocket was fired into his flat in Sarajevo. His wife was killed, and his brother, because they got confused. They thought that his brother was in fact him. He remained alone with two children. I have said this to show how cruel revenge was and how there was no forgiveness in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was no forgiveness. If someone was opposed to the Islamisation in the army, this would not be forgiven. The War Presidency, which was formed in this way, started to function, and it functioned, it operated. Every member would receive -- would be assigned certain duties. I'm not going to tire you with all these details. The witnesses will talk about all this. But what is interesting is the time at which it started to be illegitimate. It became illegitimate when, after the referendum, of which we will speak as one of the key events in the BH, the Serbs, the representatives of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, left the Assembly, left all the organs of power which were elected at the first free elections, and thus they left the Presidency too. Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic left. In accordance with the constitutional regulations, new elections should have been called. However, this was not done, but they were replaced -- well, at least form was satisfied and people were elected who were second after them according to the number of votes. Mr. Kecmanovic and Pejanovic might have been elected. However, because of the dual -- because of the games Alija Izetbegovic was playing - he was just one representative, Nenad Kecmanovic, he also left the Presidency, could no longer tolerate this, and at that time the Presidency no longer -- was no longer legitimate, just because of this, because in his place -- Don't misunderstand me. A private representative of the Serbian people came. Her name was Tatjana Ljujic-Mijatovic. She was not even in the elections for the Presidency. Alija picked her up in the street and he said, "She is a member of the Presidency." The Croats tolerated this because at the time, before the war, every situation was a stressful one and could have catastrophic consequences. It was important to preserve the peace and solve the internal political order in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a democratic way. Well, now Mr. Alija Izetbegovic replaced the legally elected representatives of the Croatian people, that is to say, Mr. Franjo Boras, because Mr. Kljuic, in the meantime, had resigned, and his resignation was accepted. So once again, new elections, but this did not take place, because Mr. Kljuic - sorry. Mr. Izetbegovic - brought in private representatives of the Croatian people, and these were Mr. Komsic, and later he again engaged Mr. Kljuic. So in these brief outlines, I don't want to tire you with this any more, but it was a farce, in brief. However, by deceiving the world, Alija Izetbegovic was manipulating with the Presidency as if it were his private presidency, and his private, personal representatives of the Serbian and Croatian people would be rewarded. They would be given various privileges. For example, they would be given big flats, they would be given important duties, and this was all taking place during the war. Children and friends could go to embassies around the world, and the like, through his unconstitutional and illegitimate way of behaving, acting. But thanks to the propaganda which was being carried out by the AID, which has been mentioned on several occasions, he, although it was totally illegitimate and though he had no legal basis, in spite of this, he governed, and in an absolute way, and would represent himself as a fighter for a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, Your Honour, although unified, it was still the property of three peoples, and because of a lack of understanding and because of the ignorance of the International Community - and this makes me sad. I can see this is present in the indictment too - because of -- for these reasons, he succeeded in presenting the situation in such a light. And the Defence - you may be certain of this, Your Honour - will call witnesses who shall contest this. I think it's half past 10.00, and Your Honours, I think you said that every hour we would be having a break. But may I just come to the end of this portion? I need five more minutes to complete this area, with the Court's indulgence. This lack of understanding, went so far, Your Honours, that for illustration purposes I'm going to talk about things that happened in this very courtroom. My learned colleagues of the Prosecution used the term "Bosnian Croat," "Bosnian Muslim." Those people don't exist. A Bosnian Croat doesn't exist, nor does a Bosnian Muslim exist as such. A Bosnian-Herzegovinian Croat and a Bosnian-Herzegovinian Muslim does exist, because the name of the state is Bosnia-Herzegovina. You will never hear, at least not witnesses that we're going to call to the courtroom, that a Muslim from Mostar will say he's a Bosnian. Heaven forbid. He's a Herzegovinian. Likewise a Croat and likewise a Serb born in Herzegovina. They will tell you the same. But when he goes outside, he says he's a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not a Bosnian Croat or a Bosnian Muslim. He doesn't use those terms. utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence will show that in 1991, precisely from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the units of the Yugoslav People's Army, still in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - it was still that at the time - under an alleged -- under the shell of -- what you say when you want to separate. Yes, secession is the word I'm looking for, secession of Croatia and Slovenia. It was precisely from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, therefore, that they attacked towns and villages and destroyed them, those belonging to the Republic of Croatia. And, if you please, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, as the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, no less proclaimed neutrality. And on state television, on the state television programme, he said that the war against Croatia was not a war of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although the JNA units were on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is from there that they attacked and occupied parts of Croatia. Now, you see, if somebody were to say that in Vienna, Paris, or New York, to make a statement like that, people would say, "Well, the President is quite right. Why not? That's a very sensible thing to do, Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why should we interfere in the war of another state?" And now look at the facts. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the situation was as follows: The Serb people, absolutely and totally armed, discarded the non-Serb elements in the JNA and thus became an absolutely Serb army. It conjoined the area which it wished to occupy in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the areas in Croatia, and to reach the borders of an imagined greater Serbia, along the lines of Virovitica, Karlobag -- Virovitica, Northern Croatia, and Karlobag, Northern Adriatic. The Muslims and Croats, totally unarmed -- as I said, there were no more weapons belonging to the TO, they had disappeared. And he says in his name, manipulating the presidency - and you'll hear that in this courtroom in due course - he says, "This isn't our war." Whose war is it, then? And by saying that, he enables the Muslims to be completely unprepared for what was to befall them and what would have happened to them had the HVO not come to their defence, had it not armed and trained the Muslims. Today, had that not happened, believe me - and even a little child knew that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what was being prepared - it is questionable what the fate and destiny of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have been, because as such, as a state, it did not exist, not only that state but neither Croatia nor Slovenia. We are talking about 1991. It was a federal unit of the Yugoslav state. To illustrate the situation and what it looked like, I'm going to show you two maps. Your Honours, here you can see from what points Croatia was attacked. This is Bosnia-Herzegovina here. This is Croatia. And the attacks were launched from all directions and axes, Vukovar, Central Croatia, Subanik [phoen], Central Dalmatia, Zadar and Dubrovnik. And now look at the result. Parts of Eastern Croatia were occupied as were Central Croatia, and all we need here is Dubrovnik. All that's missing here is Dubrovnik. We forgot to draw it in red but this part here was also occupied by the JNA or rather the Serbs, the citizens of the state of Croatia, Republic of Croatia, which was still a federal unit at that time, aided and abetted by the JNA which launched the attacks on the Croatian state. utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can move on. It's not as essential. We will be playing the tape in due course. He offered him parts which -- where the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina were the majority population. The two men refused, but the Serbs, the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a constituent peoples, took their chance and started to seize territory. What was the Croatian people to do, faced with the situation of this kind, while the state, that is to say the federal unit of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was disintegrating at the seams because the army and police were under the control of the Serbs and so were all the organs of power and authority, more or less? We are faced with a situation of total anarchy. What else could they do but guided by the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which prescribes that in case of war or immediate danger of war, immediate threat of war, the municipalities have the right and duty to organise the municipalities, to organise themselves -- I'm sorry, I said "municipalities." What I meant to say was to organise their defence, which they, in fact, did do, together with at least 30 still-free municipalities, which the Army of Republika Srpska had still not taken control of. And thus they formed the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, defending in the territory the members of all nations that found themselves in the community. Your Honour, from the declaration until the establishment of the Croatian Democratic Union, it is quite clear that that was a temporary situation for a future political order in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because at that time it still was not a state, it had not been recognised, Badinter was not there yet. We'll refer to that later. But then they said, "We're waiting for a future political solution." There was no referendum yet. The role of the HZ HB, especially after the establishment of the HVO, as an executive body, to organise the civilian and military power, especially came to the fore after the attack on Sarajevo and the blockade of Sarajevo, when the BH state, that is, the federal unit, really ceased to exist in all its aspects. Your Honour, it's very difficult for you to imagine the situation that was there at the time. We who lived through it in Zagreb, or in Croatia, and especially those who were unfortunate to experience it in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- it's very difficult to depict this. There was no electricity, water, telephones, there were no schools or companies, and the war commenced. And the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina only governed in a building that was in Sarajevo, and it wasn't even able to leave that building if it wasn't escorted by UNPROFOR, because half of Sarajevo was under blockade by the Serbian army and had been taken. Instead of the Presidency leaving the occupied Sarajevo and moving to free territory in order to oppose this aggression and to help civilian and military life, instead of doing that, it remained in its building, which it could not leave, and it could not go anywhere from that building. And you will hear witnesses who were in the immediate vicinity of Alija Izetbegovic, and they will tell you what he had to say. I'm sure that you are going to be shocked by this. The Serbs, that is to say, the Serbian people - I apologise - in Bosnia and Herzegovina, at that time they took over, they seized 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, of the federal unit. Your Honour, this is the still free territory. The red shows the occupied territory, green shows the positions where the Muslim population was in the majority, the blue shows the areas where the Croatian population was in the majority. But the HVO defended this, all of this. Have a look at the directions of attack. It was not enough. What they seized here was not enough for them. They attacked from all directions. They also attacked Jajce. And it's interesting to note that the HVO, which wanted to liberate Jajce, they were stopped at the checkpoint of army of BH in Ahmici and they were turned back. They weren't able to help Jajce. And we will produce evidence to show this. And there were a series of other strange situations. They are no longer strange today, because it was quite clear that the BH army was getting organised and it had certain objectives. They were just waiting for the Serbian aggression to stop and the help of the Croats. You will see how the situation continued to develop. As you can see, Central Bosnia here is reduced to small enclaves, and they were surrounded on all sides by Muslims and by Serbs. You'll see what happened in Mostar, what happened because of the Serbian aggression and what was liberated, and you'll see what happened in Jablanica and in Konjic. As a result of such seizure of territory, Your Honour, what happened? Have a look at this wave of refugees, where it's going. Naturally, the Croats were mostly in Herzegovina, but there were Muslims there too going to Herzegovina and to their enclaves. All the population, 80 per cent, 90 per cent of the population - please don't take this as a certain figure - all the population from the occupied parts went to the free territory. Do you know what number this is? Between 400.000 and a million. The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna took care of them in their territory, in the Republic of Croatia, in these islands, on these islands that you can see here, the islands in the Adriatic, in the hotels along the Adriatic and right up to Zagreb. They took 600.000 refugees. They took in 600.000 refugees who were of Muslim nationality and they took care of them right up until the Washington Agreement, so at the time of the so-called war too, the war between the Bosniaks and the Croats. Here we're going to show that this was not a war, that it was an attempt at aggression of the BH army, on the part of the BH army, to take as much territory as they could in order to get a head start in the negotiations and in the Vance-Owen Plan and in other negotiations too. Your Honour, Tomislavgrad, Livno, Siroki Brijeg, Mostar, Citluk. They took in -- only Mostar took in 30.000 refugees. In Siroki Brijeg, which is a small town - I will show you this - they took in about five or six thousand refugees and took care of them all the time. They took them into private houses and into homes, into the Franciscan secondary school in Siroki Brijeg, which is a well-known secondary school. We'll show you exactly who took care of them and we'll provide you with precise information, because there are even names that have been listed. They got money and other kinds of help, especially from Caritas, and only later from the Red Crescent and other humanitarian organisations and from the UNHCR. So it's clear why certain things happened in Mostar, Livno, Bugojno, how the demographic picture was upset, and it will be quite clear what direction this was heading in. The HVO resisted and it organised the Muslims for Defence. They armed Muslims. They trained them in camps in Croatia and in the HZ HB. They gave them comprehensive help in everything. So we are quite justified in saying that - and I'm going to character this a bit - the Republic of Croatia did everything in terms of arming and training the Muslims, they did everything to enable them to attack them on the following day, in the future. This is quite an exceptional case in the history of modern civilisation, isn't it? In such a situation - and we were just before the organisation of the International Community. They were about to organise - Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, although he had been warned, when he returned from the Lisbon Conference he was arrested. He was detained at the Butmir airport in Sarajevo and they took him away as a hostage. The JNA took him away as a hostage to enable the JNA to get out of its barracks which had been surrounded -- which were in the surroundings of Sarajevo and to enable him to go to Pale. We have an entire videotape which has been shown, and the entire -- all of Yugoslavia, all of former Yugoslavia watched it, because the TV participated in negotiations in a direct manner, and all of the former Yugoslavia heard this, and at that time Alija Izetbegovic illegally transferred power to Ejub Ganic. In the light of that, I tried to depict the tragedy. The Muslims didn't want to join the headquarters of the HVO and BH in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Why not? Because they were mounting a joint defence. They had weapons which were common property. They didn't want to do this, but of course we will see why, and that's when it started, in 1991. This is where the story can start, the story about the Republic of Croatia, and I will quite clearly state this here and we will use witnesses to prove this. Your Honours, if the Republic of Croatia really wanted to split up, to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina, which has been falsely said, it could have done so at any time if it had really desired to do so. Do you know on how many occasions it had to do so from the time when Alija made an offer and up until the time when they did not respond to the referendum that I'm going to mention, and right up until the agreement with the Serbs, in this chaotic situation which I have described, two peoples who were not armed and another one which was armed? But that small Croatia received 600.000 refugees. That is a very well-known fact. The entire world is aware of this. We're not going to prove this to this Tribunal. But nevertheless, we have to provide such proof. Weapons went to both Croats and Muslims in equal measure, and this free territory had to rely on Croatia so humanitarian convoys could arrive and aid could be provided to everyone in this manner. Now we have arrived at the subject of the International Community. If the Republic of Croatia had wanted to do this, it could have done so in 1991. It could have done so immediately then, because Mr. Badinter, whom the European community had appointed as an expert, could have suggested to the European community which federal units within Yugoslavia could be a state, could become a state in order to be recognised at a subsequent date. The Badinter Commission gave Slovenia and Croatia forms of statehood and the possibility of being recognised as a state. I would then have to go back in history, back to 1945 and to describe the borders of AVNOJ, but I'm not going to tire you with this. But what is interesting, Your Honours, Bosnia did not allow this. It did not allow for the possibility of becoming a state, because - this is something we're going to hear here - it was never a state in historical terms. It was never historically a state. The first time it became a state was with the recognition of the International Community, in accordance with its official borders in 1992. But Badinter didn't give Bosnia and Herzegovina the right to be a state, and as he didn't do so, the International Community had a condition. It set a certain condition for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The owners of the federal units then - the Serbs, the Muslims and the Croats, as constituent peoples and sovereign peoples, and those to whom this state belonged - if they wanted the International Community to recognise them, they should hold a referendum, and after the results of the referendum, then the International Community would come to a decision as to whether they would recognise them or not. Your Honours, the Republic of Croatia then got actively involved. All the Croatian factors in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the Croatian officials went out to the referendum and they wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina within its borders. How does a state that wants to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina act in this manner? Because when the Croats did not respond to the referendum, because the Serbs refused to respond to the referendum, because they had a plebiscite before the referendum at which they voted against a referendum because they didn't want Bosnia and Herzegovina within the borders that it has now and that it has had since 1945. So without the response of the Croats in Bosnia, Bosnia wouldn't be what it is today. This Tribunal would not exist either, and who knows what course history would have taken then. So if Croatia wanted to do so, it could have done so then. It didn't, though. And since that time, Your Honour, it is not possible to say that the Croats wanted a division of any kind. Whoever does that is ill-intentioned and is deceptive. That was a crucial moment in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So first of all it armed and then liberated, it responded to a referendum. If Croatia had had such a plan, it would not have acted in this manner. I think that this is quite clear. And after that date, from that date onward, it is no longer possible to talk about the desire of Croatia to divide Bosnia. Thanks to the Croats and to Croatian votes, the referendum was successful, and in April 1992 the International Community finally recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina. But look, only within its external borders but not its political order. This is something that was left to negotiations which were to follow, and how those three peoples would order their state was something to be decided later. Then there were negotiations, the London Conference, the Geneva Conference, the Vance-Owen Plan, Owen Stoltenberg, et cetera, and I will talk about this later. All these negotiations related to how these three peoples would order this state, whether it would be a cantonal system, as in Switzerland, whether it would be organised into provinces, unions of republics, federal units, et cetera. This was something that was to be left for subsequent negotiations, and this is something that the three constituent peoples had to agree on. Defence will use experts and witnesses to show -- to prove the following facts too. At the moment, the HZ HB, so within the external borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it organised its life and it was waiting to see how it would agree with others on the future political order. And we are charged with the fact that they were using the Croatian language, but what language were they supposed to use? And do you know what language is used in Herzegovina by Herzegovinians? And I said they were both Muslims and Croats and Serbs. It's mostly Croatian because the Croatian grammar and language is based on the speech in Herzegovina, the Stokavian dialect, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which is used there. I don't know how this will be translated. This is the purest form of the Croatian language and it is this form of the Croatian language which is spoken there in that part. And gentlemen, we will use proof to -- evidence to prove this story about the language. There is no such thing as a Bosnian language. It doesn't exist in constitutional or legal terms. This is a well-known fact. Everyone knows this. Serbo-Croat is used - that's the language which exists - or Croato-Serbian. In schools, they would write in the Latin script for one week and they would write in the Cyrillic script for the second week. And, Your Honours, for language to be language, it has to have certain preconditions. It has to have a grammar, it has to have rules, in order for it to constitute a language. You can see that these are false requests, made up requests, the purpose of which is only to create division, and when they received -- when the Bosniak language was recognised by the Washington Agreement, they no longer want to call it the Bosniak language, they now want to say that that's a mistake and they want to say that it's the Bosnian language, not the Bosniak language. I don't know how the translators can translate this now. So the difference between the Bosniaks and the Bosnians, that is to say between Bosnian -- the Bosnian and the Bosniak language, and you know they now have a certain grammar for the Bosnian language, I don't know in fact whether it exists now, but it's the same language, of course, but there are a lot of terms from the Arabic, a lot of terms from Turkish, which have been introduced, and that's the only difference. Everyone, anyone who is normal in Bosnia-Herzegovina, will tell you that this Bosnian language now is in fact the same language, and especially this was especially the case up to 1994. Of course it was only one language. So we are being charged with -- for having used the Croatian money in the HZ HB. Anyone who knows about history will know that money is -- that the only holy money in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the German mark, which is the case today, the only currency that was respected. And in that war chaos which I have just described, all forms of currency were used. However, we will provide evidence, Your Honour, to prove that. I don't want to go into closed session and just mention the name, but a witness will appear, will come here, and he will tell you what happened with regard to currency and that the HZ HB never had a national bank, and if it didn't have a national bank, it didn't have monetary policies either, fiscal policies. If it had no fiscal policies, then that means that it didn't have a currency of its own either. And the Croatian money, the Croatian dinar which later became the Croatian kuna, was in use, as were all other currencies, as were any other currencies. And what I further want to state in my opening statement, when we are talking about the Croatian Community in Herceg-Bosna and about the allegations of the Prosecutor, one of the objectives was -- that one of the objectives was also to establish closer ties with Croatia, so what is illegal in this case? Why should this be criminal? Well, of course, of course they would want to have close ties, and even today they want to. Its parent unit is over the border. The problem of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina is -- and of the Serbian people, is that their parent countries are right behind their backs, and we will show that the Bosniak people has a parent unit too, which unites them, but it's a bit -- it's further removed from them. Your Honour, I'm selecting this term, the constitutional provisions of the Republic of Croatia was that it is necessary to take care of Croats wherever they are throughout the world. And any democratic country would do this. It's normal. They would take care of their citizens, they would take care of their rights in other states, and so on and so forth. And such cooperation, luckily until quite recently, was excellent. And now this right too - and here there is a lot of deception, one is being guided by deceptions - in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which even today is not a unified country, a state, because it is made up of two units, two federal units, there is an international governor who is in charge, who interprets the provisions, the rules, as he wishes. And thus quite recently, within those rules, the Croatian Television was shut down, the transmitters were closed down, so people are no longer able to watch broadcasts. This happened in 2001, and it was the decision of the international community, of the governor who represents the international community in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if there were free elections and the people chose their representatives, and the governor then said, "Well, we don't recognise this because they are nationalists," what then? These were all legally elected representatives in 2001, and they were all replaced. Well, that's just -- those are just a few brief comments about democracy and about close ties with Croatia, but you will hear more about this. I think, Your Honours, that while straying a bit - I have a note here to bring me back to my topic - when I said that the TO did not want to have a common headquarters with the HVO except in Mostar, Herzegovina was an exemplary community of good cooperation between the Muslims and Croats until some historical events that I'll talk about later on. But all I wish to illustrate with this was that in 1992, in July and December -- from May to December, sorry, take a look at this. May, December, 1992. These are incidents exclusively - I refer to them as incidents - of the BH Army towards the HVO, Kresovo, the 17th of June, 1992; Fojnica, June, 1992; Kiseljak, the 20th of October, et cetera, et cetera. All in 1992, from the month of May to the month of December. Let's move on, and we'll see how we are going to refute all the premises put forward by the Prosecution. I don't think, Your Honours, you have yet had occasion to see a map like this. This is September, 1992. Look at the situation in Central Bosnia, and some of the Prosecution witnesses spoke about the situation. Look at the situation. This blue colour, this blue area, are the Croatian enclaves. This is territory under the control of the BH Army, and this was under Serb control. So no points in common with no connections with free territory, HZ HB. They have been completely separated. And that was the case right up to the Washington Agreements. And these red dots here, the ones that you can see on the edges of those enclaves, are where the BiH Army attacks on the enclaves. And it is logical why it would be nice to unify all this. They use the term "liberate." Who were they liberating the enclave from? Because the population was 90 per cent Croats. How do they have the right to say that they are liberating something, a community of three nations, the BH Army is proclaiming the liberation of Bosnia. So they are going to liberate Vitez and Busovaca, are they, from the Croats? So are they liberating them from the Croats whereas the population is 90 per cent Croat in that area? But let's move on, Your Honours. I have an English text here, and signatures. This is a Prosecution exhibit, P318, and I have placed the 20th of April, 1993, there on purpose, and this document stipulates the following: [In English] Both legal and military forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they are treated equally. [Interpretation] This was signed by, if you please, [In English] BH Army Commander-in-Chief, Sefer Halilovic, HVO Commander-in-Chief, Milivoj Petkovic, Commander UN, B and H command, General Philip Morillon, the ECMM, [Interpretation] stationed in Zenica, the main headquarters in Zenica. You know what came before this agreement, long before either agreement. Here it is, we have it once again in English. Yes, we do. It was preceded by a prior agreement signed a long time previously, on the 28th of July, 1992, in fact, in Zagreb, and its annex signed in New York, and it is Exhibit P159, and it represents an agreement between the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was recognised at that time in its foreign borders, its external borders, and the Republic of Croatia, a state that had already been recognised by the international community, that is to say the state of Croatia. And the agreement is an agreement on friendship and cooperation in which the HVO was proclaimed and equated to the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. And now we come to another important topic. Military cooperation was agreed upon between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia for the second time, and that military agreement was confirmed by the Split agreement, and later on, in 1995, reasserted with the associated forces of BiH and ABiH when they liberated a large portion of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why am I pointing this out to you, Your Honours? The state of Croatia had the absolute right, according to international rules and regulations, in view of the fact that it was attacked by another state, to enter into that territory in depth and to neutralise fire. It did not do so. According to this military agreement, the HVO could legally have entered Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it did not go there. You know when it went there? The HV, I mean, the HV, the Croatian army is what I'm referring to. Although it could have on the basis of this agreement, it was called to arrive, but it came after Srebrenica, Your Honours. That's when it arrived. Srebrenica took place in 1995. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina publicly, in front of this -- before this international court of law did not pull out a single corps towards the Drina border to save Srebrenica and the Muslims in Eastern Herzegovina. All its force, about 200.000 men, you know where they were concentrated? It concentrated them in the Zenica and Tuzla basin with the intent of attacking central Bosnia. And the 6th and 4th Corps, Konjic-Mostar, won over, which was its goal, the whole Neretva Valley, from Jablanica to Konjic, and this is what they did - and later on, in due course, we will demonstrate that to you - the final goal being seizing Mostar, taking over Mostar, and there is a clear order that we are going to authenticate very easily about the attack on Mostar on the 16th of April, 1993, and this came to pass on the 9th of May, 1993, and all this was an introduction into a plan which was called, "Neretva 1993," which was given form to by the supreme commander, and ordered by him, thought up by the main headquarters, and the object was to come out on to the sea, on to the coast in the town of Neum, and for them to be able to accomplish that, that Mostar had to be taken control of. Mr. Sefer Halilovic who was no longer the commander but the main inspector of the BH Army, describes this in detail in a book he published. And this is the book. And that is when the worst crimes were committed, without any objection, I hope, from the Prosecution, the crimes against Croats. That is when there was ethnic cleansing of the whole area of Jablanica-Konjic, and the most horrendous crimes took place in the town of Grabovica, where 35 civilians were massacred -- and I apologise for having to say this. I'm going to give a terrible example. People were impaled and put up on the cross as well. When the Defence is bringing this up, we don't expect, and we promise not to have a tu quoque Defence, nor would I allow this to take place, but I have to explain certain events, because nothing drops from the sky just like that. Nothing is parachuted down. And that I say just for the purposes of illustration. To wind up with the HVO -- with the HV, Your Honour, when the Republic of Croatia was attacked in September, 1991, in what was then a joint state, the state of Yugoslavia, and a fact that we are going to present to this Court, which is that Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time lived in the state of Croatia, and born -- the first generation born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so just those -- the first generation ones. There were 400.000 of them, and what happened? A very logical thing. All the Croats from Bosnia, Croatia, came into Croatia to defend their parents, to defend their brethren, to defend their relatives, to defend their friends, and in order to do so they had to enter, but only in 1992, because Croatia still did not have an army of its own. And it was organised through police formations or the guards or the Zenga, in 1992, and after that, the Croatian army was established. These young men joined the Croatian army. To be brief, in 1992 the position was a logical one. When their thresholds were attacked, the relatives in Bosnia-Herzegovina and family members and friends, meant that these young men returned to their thresholds. They were now already citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But together with them came their brothers, fathers, relatives, and friends, who were citizens of the RH and citizens of the RBIH by virtue of their birth, and dual nationality was recognised and made legal by the agreement I showed you a moment ago, and it applied to both Croats and Muslims alike. They came to Bosnia-Herzegovina to defend it. Yes, they did, of course. And what happened next? Nobody is going to take off an HV insignia, because he is from the Croatian army. The Croatian army was just being organised. In April 1992 was when the Serb aggression began. And just as the fighting in Croatia stopped with the advent of UNPROFOR around that time, in April 1992, the war stopped in Croatia, thanks to UNPROFOR and the International Community, but the occupied portions of territory remained, which were liberated in 1995. So it is these young men who arrived, and they're not going to take off their insignias, because they were proud of being members of the army. They said they had been members for so many years, and nobody minded, until somebody suddenly thought: Well, this might be an aggression. And that's when the whole story about the Croatian army started. But the story didn't start off by saying that Canada and America and France effected the aggression, because there were at least 30 ethnic Croats who were citizens of Canada, the United States, countries in Europe. Nobody says that. Whereas they were citizens of those countries. But these were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina temporarily fighting in Croatia, and then they went back and then they were demobilised, they were released from the HV, and the others arrived as volunteers, their brothers and relatives and brethren from Croatia having dual nationality. Similarly, Your Honours, nobody ever said: Well, why is Sefer Halilovic the citizen of another state? But Slobodan Praljak was -- people did say, "Well, he came from the HV." Yes, he did. He did come from the HV. Do you know where Mr. Praljak was born? In Capljina. And he spent his entire life in Siroki Brijeg. When he saw what was happening, he was demobilised, and not only him as an officer, but other officers were demobilised too, just like the members of the Foreign Legion, the French state, and they were ethnic Croats who were let go straight away, although they had French citizenship. The French Foreign Legion let them go for them to be able to fight in their homeland, because to defend one's homeland is a point of honour, and it is one's duty as well. But we will demonstrate all that before this Trial Chamber in this courtroom in due course. Yes. Perhaps we could take a break. I wanted to get through as much as possible, but I've been reminded that perhaps this is an opportune moment.
